title: Developer Experience: SDK Guides, Quickstarts, API Examples, Docs Site Ops & Top Issues
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This page describes the standards, templates, operating procedures, and canonical fixes maintained by the Developer Experience (DevEx) team for SDK guides, quickstarts, API examples, docs-site operations, and the list of top support issues. The goal is to make documentation consistent, discoverable, and low-friction for developers integrating with Redwood Inference.

Goals
- Provide canonical, production-ready SDK guides and quickstarts for Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Go.
- Ensure API examples are minimal, copy/paste-ready, and cover common patterns (chat, streaming, embeddings, function calling).
- Maintain a reproducible docs-site publishing flow with SLOs for review and publication.
- Surface and maintain canonical fixes for the 20 most common support issues seen by DevEx and Support.

Audience
- SDK authors and maintainers
- Solutions engineers and support engineers
- Product and platform engineers who need consistent docs for customers

Scope
This document covers: templates and examples, how to write and review docs, publishing procedures for the docs site, triage and canonical fixes for top support issues, and ownership/SLAs. It does NOT cover product PRD or marketing copy (see related pages).

Templates and authoring standards
All DevEx docs should follow these conventions:
- Headings: use clear, short headings. Prefer present-tense verbs (e.g., \"Install the SDK\").
- Intro: each page begins with a one-paragraph summary and a short scope section.
- Code samples: provide at least one minimal curl example and one SDK example in each supported language.
- Commands: mark OS-specific commands (macOS/Linux vs Windows).
- Troubleshooting: include a short \"Troubleshooting\" section with signals and canonical fixes.
- Ownership & cadence: add an \"Owner\" line and a quarterly review date in the metadata.

SDK Guide (required sections)
1) Title and short summary (1-2 sentences)
2) Supported versions (SDK and API) and compatibility notes
3) Quick installation (copy/paste commands)
4) Minimal example (one request that demonstrates the most common use case)
5) Advanced topics: streaming, retries/backoff, batching, auth, telemetry
6) Migration notes (breaking changes, deprecations)
7) Troubleshooting and top issues
8) API reference links and sample prompts/fixtures

Quickstart template (user flow)
1) Goal: what the quickstart will accomplish (e.g., \"Embed your product catalog and query with nearest neighbors\")
2) Prerequisites: account, API key, SDK version, environment variables
3) Install: commands for pip/npm/go get etc.
4) Minimal end-to-end example (5-10 lines where possible)
5) Validation: how to confirm it worked (sample outputs/assertions)
6) Next steps: links to advanced guides and performance tips

API examples and patterns
- Provide a canonical curl example for each endpoint (generation, chat, streaming, embeddings, reranking). Keep headers and payloads minimal and realistic.
- Provide SDK examples for Python, JS/TS, and Go. Prefer composition over abstraction: short examples that are easy to grep and copy.
- Include a streaming example with client-side pseudocode and server-side considerations (timeouts, chunk sizing).

Canonical curl example (chat, short):

curl -X POST \
  https://api.redwood-inference.internal/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-1-chat","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the following..."}],"max_tokens":200}'

Python SDK minimal (example):

from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"))
resp = client.chat.create(model="redwood-1-chat", messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}], max_tokens=100)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Docs site operating procedures (publishing & reviews)
- Branch + PR workflow: authors create a branch under devex/* and open a PR that targets docs-site/main. PR title format: \"docs(devex): <short desc>\".
- Review SLA: PRs tagged with \"docs-review\" should be reviewed within 5 business days. Emergency fixes have a 24-hour SLA.
- Staging preview: every PR must render on staging (staging.docs.redwood-inference) and include a short checklist in the PR description: staging URL, screenshots, and smoke-test steps.
- Publish window: we publish on Mondays at 09:00 PT to minimize cross-team conflicts. For critical security or billing changes, request an off-cycle release via #devex-release with approval from at least one reviewer.
- Rollback: rollback is performed by reverting the merge commit and rerunning the site build. Notify #devex-alerts and file a post-release check within 24 hours.

Content ownership and cadence
- Owners must add a quarterly review date in the page metadata. The DevEx team runs a documentation audit each quarter to identify stale or high-traffic pages that need updates.
- Metrics to track: page views, time-to-first-byte for code samples, number of support tickets referencing the page, and search success rate (click-throughs from internal site search).

Top support issues and canonical fixes (current top 12)
1) Authentication errors (401/403)
   - Symptom: API returns 401 or 403 for valid-looking requests.
   - Root cause: expired or mistyped API key; mixing sandbox vs production keys; missing organization header for enterprise customers.
   - Canonical fix: rotate key, ensure REDWOOD_API_KEY env var is set and not prefixed with \"Bearer \". For enterprise, include header X-Redwood-Org: <org-id>. Add suggested curl to troubleshooting.

2) Rate-limit or 429 errors
   - Symptom: requests intermittently receive 429s under load.
   - Root cause: burst traffic exceeding per-route quotas or missing client-side exponential backoff.
   - Canonical fix: implement retry with jitter (base=200ms, max=4s), batch requests where possible, and file a support ticket to increase quota for Dedicated accounts.

3) Streaming cutoffs / truncated responses
   - Symptom: streaming responses end prematurely or clients time out.
   - Root cause: client read timeouts, proxy idle timeouts (e.g., NGINX default), or missing keepalive headers.
   - Canonical fix: increase client and proxy timeouts to 120s for long responses; ensure chunked transfer encoding is preserved.

4) High latency for short completions
   - Symptom: sub-200-token responses take >300ms higher than expected.
   - Root cause: client-side batching disabled; request routed to cold model instance.
   - Canonical fix: enable client-side batching and set model routing hints (prefer low-latency variants) in request metadata.

5) Incorrect embeddings shape / dtype mismatches
   - Symptom: library errors when using embedding vectors for nearest-neighbor indexers.
   - Root cause: mismatch between model embedding size and indexer schema; dtype conversion (float64 vs float32).
   - Canonical fix: confirm model embedding dims using /v1/models/<model-id> and cast arrays to float32 before indexing. Add example using numpy.astype('float32').

6) Authorization header formatting issues
   - Symptom: 401s when using SDKs or scripts.
   - Root cause: accidentally including quotes or additional text around the token.
   - Canonical fix: use Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN (no quotes), or prefer SDK that injects header automatically.

7) Function calling mismatches
   - Symptom: model returns free-text instead of invoking provided function schema.
   - Root cause: schema invalid (wrong types), or field names mismatched.
   - Canonical fix: validate function JSON Schema locally (jsonschema.validate) and include a minimal function-calling example in the SDK guide.

8) Model compatibility / deprecation surprises
   - Symptom: previously working prompt yields degraded output after model change.
   - Root cause: automatic model fallback or a new default model with different behavior.
   - Canonical fix: pin model version in customer configs and add migration notes for new model variants.

9) Incorrect content-type (multipart vs application/json)
   - Symptom: 400 errors when uploading files or binary payloads.
   - Root cause: wrong Content-Type header or missing boundary.
   - Canonical fix: use multipart/form-data with correct boundary and recommend SDK helper methods that wrap file uploads.

10) Embeddings drift/regression
   - Symptom: search relevance drops for a customer workload after model upgrade.
   - Root cause: model embedding changes or indexing pipeline mismatch.
   - Canonical fix: re-index corpus, run A/B evals with sample queries, and follow Redwood Optimize recommendations for quantization and model selection.

11) Billing spikes after bulk ingestion
   - Symptom: unexpected high token/embedding usage after a big data import.
   - Root cause: accidental replays without batching or missing caching policies.
   - Canonical fix: enable deduplication, batch requests, and use cost-estimate tooling in Redwood Console; open a billing support ticket if spike is unexpected.

12) Local dev environment mismatches
   - Symptom: quickstarts work locally but fail in CI due to env differences.
   - Root cause: missing environment variables, different SDK versions, or network egress restrictions in CI.
   - Canonical fix: include a reproducible Dockerfile or GitHub Actions job in quickstarts and pin SDK versions in requirements files.

Each entry above should be copied into the specific SDK guide and quickstart troubleshooting sections where relevant. Keep the canonical fix text short and include a one-line reproduction command where possible.

Release checklist for docs and examples
- Update changelog for SDK and docs (if breaking changes).
- Smoke test examples on staging and include staging URL in PR.
- Run quick automated tests: 1) curl example returns 200; 2) Python example executes without exceptions; 3) Build succeeds locally.
- Tag the PR with affected SDK(s) and whether this is a security/billing/policy change.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: DevEx (eng-developer-experience). Assign secondary owners for each language SDK (Python, JS/TS, Go).
- Escalation path: DevEx -> SDK Lead -> Eng Platform -> Security (for incidents involving keys/data).
- For customer-impacting documentation errors, follow the oncall-and-incident-response incident process and create a support ticket linking to the doc and the canonical fix.

Appendix: Example SDK guide (Python minimal)

Title: \"Python SDK Quickstart: chat with Redwood-1\"
Summary: One-paragraph summary: this quickstart shows how to install the Python SDK and run a simple chat completion.
Prereqs: Python 3.9+, REDWOOD_API_KEY set in your environment.
Install: pip install redwood-inference
Minimal example:

import os
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY"))
resp = client.chat.create(model="redwood-1-chat", messages=[{"role":"user","content":"Explain event sourcing in 3 sentences."}], max_tokens=120)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Troubleshooting:
- 401: confirm REDWOOD_API_KEY is correct and not wrapped in quotes.
- 429: add exponential backoff with jitter.

Appendix: Quickstart CI example (GitHub Actions)
- Provide a short workflow that runs the Python quickstart in a sandbox using a short-lived token (rotate tokens between runs).

Notes and next steps
- Keep this page updated with any canonical fixes discovered during support rotations.
- Quarterly audit owner: @Aisha (DevEx).
